analysis.one_liner: Requires pardon recipients to disclose money or benefits they gave the President or his family.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on August 3, 2026 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has received no hearing, no markup, and no vote; Congress adjourns in January 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets pay-to-play pardons. It would require anyone who receives a presidential pardon, commutation, or reprieve to report to the Justice Department, on a public website, any money or benefits worth $10,000 or more that they gave to the President, his family, or entities tied to them — including campaign committees, presidential libraries, and family businesses — going back to a year before the President took office and covering four years afterward. It would also update the federal bribery law to say explicitly that the President and Vice President are covered officials and that a pardon counts as a "thing of value," with a 10-year window to prosecute pardon-related bribery. Violations carry civil fines up to $50,000 and up to 5 years in prison for willful false or missing reports.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who rely on the justice system's integrity: the public would see a searchable record of who paid what to the President's orbit before or after receiving clemency. Honest clemency applicants, who follow the Justice Department process for years without results while connected insiders get fast-tracked, would benefit from a pardon system that is harder to sell. Federal prosecutors would get a clearer bribery statute and a longer window to bring cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens and honest clemency applicants

how_it_helps.text: Any clemency recipient who provided a benefit worth $10,000 or more to the President, an immediate family member, or an entity advancing the President's financial, political, or reputational interests must file a disclosure report with the Attorney General within 90 days, then annually for four more years.
The Attorney General must publish all disclosure reports on a searchable, machine-readable public Justice Department website within 30 days of each filing deadline.

The bill amends the federal bribery statute to state that the President and Vice President are covered officials and that a pardon, commutation, reprieve, or remission of fines is 'anything of value,' and adds a 10-year statute of limitations for bribery offenses involving executive clemency.

Violations carry a civil penalty of up to $50,000 per violation, and willfully failing to file or filing a materially false report is punishable by up to 5 years in prison; the Attorney General is given explicit authority to investigate and enforce.

The bill's findings argue that presidential clemency has been used to reward donors, allies, and well-connected offenders while ordinary petitioners wait years in the Justice Department process, and that pardons wiped out nearly $2 billion in victim repayments and taxpayer recovery.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy or well-connected people seeking pardons and the lobbyists and intermediaries who broker clemency for them would bear new disclosure duties, legal exposure, and public scrutiny of the payments they route to the President's family, businesses, foundations, and political committees. Payments to pardon lobbyists would no longer be sheltered under the legal-services exception. Incumbent presidents and their families lose the ability to receive money from clemency recipients without a public paper trail.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wealthy pardon seekers and clemency lobbyists

drawbacks.text: The disclosure duty falls entirely on clemency recipients, not on the President or his family; the bill itself acknowledges that the President's own conduct may be beyond federal prosecution after the Supreme Court's immunity decision in Trump v. United States, so the core actor faces no new obligation.

Enforcement depends entirely on the Attorney General of the day, who would be the same administration official the bill is aimed at influencing — an Attorney General who declines to investigate faces no penalty under this law.

Recipients must decide in good faith how to allocate payments between protected legal fees and disclosable clemency-related lobbying, a judgment call that creates compliance costs and could chill legitimate legal representation.

The bill targets one President's conduct by name in its findings, which invites challenge on the ground that Congress is directing criminal law at a single administration rather than setting a general rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but bounded by design: a public record of money flowing to a President's circle from pardon recipients would expose pay-to-play clemency that is currently invisible, and the explicit statement that a pardon is a bribe-able 'thing of value' matters even if prosecutions are rare. The honest weaknesses are that it polices the buyers of pardons rather than the seller, and that it relies on the Justice Department to enforce against the very administration it polices. As an anti-corruption measure it is a transparency tool, not a cure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Judiciary Committee when it was introduced in August 2026 and has sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote as the Congress heads toward its January 2027 end.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph Morelle introduced the bill on August 3, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
Nine Democratic colleagues signed on as cosponsors; no Republican is listed.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action since the referral.
The 119th Congress remains in session until January 3, 2027, so the bill is not yet dead, but a bill with no committee action in its first months rarely reaches the floor in time.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has gone nowhere, the current system continues as it is: pardon recipients face no requirement to disclose what they gave the President or his family, the bribery statute still does not name the President, and the conduct the bill's findings describe remains lawful and unreported. The status quo benefits whoever holds clemency power and the well-connected people who can access it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The President's orbit and well-connected pardon recipients

for.name: Rep. Joseph Morelle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 3, 2026 and described in its findings a pattern of clemency traded for money and political benefit.

for.name: 9 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Added their names in support of the bill upon introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership (Chair Jim Jordan)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — leaving it without a path to the floor.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party control of floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a House floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters — the sponsor and nine cosponsors — are Democrats, and the bill's findings are aimed squarely at a Republican president; no Republican has signed on.

industries.note: The bill strips legal-services protection from payments made for clemency-related lobbying and advocacy, forcing disclosure of what clients pay pardon brokers and capping nothing about their fees but ending their invisibility. A business built on quietly selling access to the clemency process loses its main asset: opacity.

industries.industry: Presidential family businesses, foundations, and political committees
industries.note: Entities advancing the President's financial, political, or reputational interests — including family businesses, presidential libraries, inaugural committees, and campaign committees — are defined as covered recipients, so money they receive from future clemency recipients would have to appear on a public Justice Department website. Their interest in remaining undisclosed runs directly against the public's interest in seeing who pays whom.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action more than a month into its life, only Democratic cosponsors, and a House majority controlled by the party of the President it targets, the realistic path to a floor vote is essentially closed before the January 2027 adjournment; the most it could achieve is attention if attached to unrelated legislation, which is unlikely.
